collection: NECO Geography map skills and human geography practice
note: Original structured practice. Map calculations use supplied measurements. Official objectives remain unverified and academic review is pending.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied map measurements and terrain evidence to calculate and interpret distances, gradients and routes.
questions.prompt: A straight path between a clinic and a bridge measures 7.6 cm on a 1:25,000 map. Calculate the straight-line ground distance in kilometres.

markingGuide.description: Convert one map centimetre to 250 m on the ground.
Multiply by 7.6 to obtain 1,900 m.
Convert to 1.9 km.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied map measurements and terrain evidence to calculate and interpret distances, gradients and routes.
questions.prompt: Two points on a mapped footpath have heights of 315 m and 195 m. Their horizontal ground separation is 1.8 km. Calculate the average gradient as 1 in n, and state which point is uphill from the other.
questions.answer: 1 in 15. The 315 m point is uphill from the 195 m point.
questions.explanation: 1 in 15. The 315 m point is uphill from the 195 m point.

markingGuide.description: Find the vertical difference of 120 m.
Convert the horizontal distance to 1,800 m and divide by 120.
Give 1 in 15 and the correct uphill direction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied map measurements and terrain evidence to calculate and interpret distances, gradients and routes.
questions.prompt: Two equal-length map segments cross slopes with the same contour interval. Segment A crosses six contour intervals and segment B crosses two. The heights change steadily along each segment. Which segment has the steeper average slope, and why?
questions.answer: Segment A. It has a larger vertical change over the same horizontal distance.
questions.explanation: Segment A. It has a larger vertical change over the same horizontal distance.

markingGuide.description: Identify segment A.
Use equal contour intervals to link the crossing count to vertical change.
Explain why greater vertical change over the same distance means steeper gradient.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied map measurements and terrain evidence to calculate and interpret distances, gradients and routes.
questions.prompt: A map shows Route A as 2 km long with a total climb of 140 m, and Route B as 3 km long with a total climb of 35 m. Both routes are open. A group wants to minimise climbing even if it walks farther. Recommend a route and explain one limit of the map data for planning.
questions.answer: Choose B because it has less total climbing. Total climb and route length do not show how steep the steepest short section is.
questions.explanation: Choose B because it has less total climbing. Total climb and route length do not show how steep the steepest short section is.

markingGuide.description: Select B using the stated priority.
Compare the climbs of 35 m and 140 m.
Identify a valid missing detail, such as maximum gradient or surface condition.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Use supplied map measurements and terrain evidence to calculate and interpret distances, gradients and routes.
questions.prompt: A printed map at 1:40,000 is photocopied at 80% of its original linear size. Calculate the new representative fraction.

markingGuide.description: Explain that 0.8 cm on the copy represents the original 1 cm.
Divide the original scale denominator by 0.8 to obtain 50,000.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Infer settlement patterns and functions from evidence and explain migration decisions.
questions.prompt: In a fictional village, most houses stand beside a raised road through seasonally wet farmland. Name the settlement pattern and explain how both the road and wet ground can help account for it.
questions.answer: A linear settlement. The road provides access and its raised strip offers drier building sites than the adjacent fields.
questions.explanation: A linear settlement. The road provides access and its raised strip offers drier building sites than the adjacent fields.

markingGuide.description: Identify the linear pattern.
Link the road to access or movement.
Link the wet surroundings to concentration on higher ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Infer settlement patterns and functions from evidence and explain migration decisions.
questions.prompt: A council must choose a weekly market site. Site A is at the road junction but floods regularly. Site B is slightly farther away on dry ground and has a bus stop. If the priority is reliable trading in the rainy season, recommend a site and discuss one trade-off.
questions.answer: Choose B for reliable access to a dry site. It loses some junction traffic or requires a longer journey for some traders, although the bus stop helps.
questions.explanation: Choose B for reliable access to a dry site. It loses some junction traffic or requires a longer journey for some traders, although the bus stop helps.

markingGuide.description: Select B using the stated priority.
Link dry ground to fewer weather-related interruptions.
Explain a plausible access or visibility cost.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Infer settlement patterns and functions from evidence and explain migration decisions.
questions.prompt: A town has a large produce depot and several truck repair yards. A nearby village mainly has homes and fields. Explain one commercial function and one transport-related function of the town using the evidence.
questions.answer: The depot supports collecting and distributing produce. The repair yards service vehicles used in moving goods.
questions.explanation: The depot supports collecting and distributing produce. The repair yards service vehicles used in moving goods.

markingGuide.description: Use the depot to infer a commercial function.
Use the repair yards to infer a transport-support function.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Infer settlement patterns and functions from evidence and explain migration decisions.
questions.prompt: A family leaves a village after two failed harvests and settles in a city because one parent has found paid work there. Identify the type of migration and distinguish the push factor from the pull factor.
questions.answer: Rural-to-urban migration. Crop failure is the push factor and the city job is the pull factor.
questions.explanation: Rural-to-urban migration. Crop failure is the push factor and the city job is the pull factor.

markingGuide.description: Classify the migration as rural-to-urban.
Identify failed harvests as the pressure at origin.
Identify paid work as the attraction at destination.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.learningObjective: Infer settlement patterns and functions from evidence and explain migration decisions.
questions.prompt: A school survey counts pupils who cross into a nearby town each morning and return home in the afternoon. A report calls this permanent migration. Evaluate that label and say what evidence would support a claim of permanent migration.
questions.answer: The trips are commuting because the pupils return to their usual homes. Evidence of a lasting change of usual residence would support permanent migration.
questions.explanation: The trips are commuting because the pupils return to their usual homes. Evidence of a lasting change of usual residence would support permanent migration.

markingGuide.description: Distinguish regular commuting from relocation.
Identify evidence of a lasting change of usual residence.
